name: Maize
summary: Farmers of southern Mexico breed a wild grass, teosinte, into maize, a plant that can no longer seed itself without people. It becomes the staple of the Americas from the St Lawrence to the Andes, and after 1492 one of the staples of the world.

spread.note: Maize reaches the Andes, where it is grown on terraces and brewed into chicha beer.
Columbus brings maize home from his first voyage, and Peter Martyr describes it the same year.
Portuguese ships carry it on to Africa and Asia.
Hieronymus Bock describes 'foreign corn' in his herbal; many in Europe think it came from Turkey.
Portuguese traders bring maize to the Gulf of Guinea, where it becomes a staple of the forest kingdoms.
First written down in China in a county gazetteer, as 'imperial wheat'. Within two centuries it feeds settlers in the hills of the interior.
Portuguese traders bring it to Kyushu.
Maize spreads from China into the northern hills.
Maize becomes the staple that feeds Cahokia and the mound towns.
Maize is grown with beans and squash, the Three Sisters.
Maize is grown across the Ottoman lands; much of Europe calls it 'Turkish corn'.
Lopes describes maize in Kongo as 'Mazza Manputo', the grain of Portugal.
Portuguese and Spanish ships bring maize to the islands of the spice trade.
Maize is grown in India, brought by the Portuguese.

name: The potato
summary: Farmers around Lake Titicaca domesticate a wild tuber that thrives at heights where maize fails, and learn to freeze-dry it into chuño, which keeps for years. Carried to Europe, it fed the growing cities of the eighteenth century; Ireland's dependence on it ended in the famine of 1845.

spread.note: Potatoes reach Spain from Peru; Seville's Hospital de la Sangre is buying them in 1573.
John Gerard pictures the potato in his Herball, calling it, wrongly, the potato of Virginia.
Olivier de Serres describes the 'cartoufle' in his treatise on farming; France is slow to eat it until Parmentier's campaign of the 1770s.
Dutch and Portuguese ships bring the potato to Nagasaki; it is named jagaimo, the Jakarta tuber.
Potatoes are served at a feast for the English ambassador at the Mughal court.
Potatoes reach China by sea and are grown in the hills of the south-east.
Catherine the Great's Senate orders instructions on growing potatoes sent across the empire.
Potatoes come across the Tumen from Manchuria.

name: The sweet potato
summary: A tropical American root that crossed the Pacific twice: once in Polynesian canoes centuries before Columbus, and again in the Manila galleons, to become the food that kept south China alive through famine.

spread.note: Charred sweet potato in a Mangaia rock shelter shows it reached Polynesia long before Europeans, carried back, most likely, by Polynesian voyagers who reached South America. Its name, kumara, echoes the Quechua cumal.
The first settlers of New Zealand bring kumara, and learn to store it through a winter the tropics never had.
Columbus finds the batata in the Caribbean. Its Taíno name, carried to Europe, became the English 'potato'.
Portuguese and Spanish ships bring the sweet potato to the Moluccas.
The Manila galleons bring it across the Pacific from Mexico to the Spanish Philippines.
Chen Zhenlong smuggles vines from Luzon wound into a ship's rope. When famine strikes Fujian the next year, the governor has them planted.
Noguni Sōkan brings it home to Okinawa from Fujian.
Maeda Riemon brings it from Ryukyu to Satsuma; in Japan it is still called satsuma-imo.
The envoy Jo Eom brings sweet potatoes back from Tsushima as a famine crop.

name: The chili pepper
summary: Domesticated in Mexico and eaten across the Americas, the chili took less than a century after 1492 to become part of the cooking of India, Southeast Asia and much of Africa, and later of Sichuan and Hunan.

spread.note: Columbus calls it pimiento, taking it for a kind of black pepper, the spice he had sailed to find.
Portuguese ships take it on to Africa and Asia.
Chilies spread through the Ottoman lands, and from there to Hungary.
Chilies reach the Portuguese at Goa. Within a century they are grown across India and are a staple of its cooking.
The Portuguese bring it to Kyushu, where it is called tōgarashi, 'Chinese mustard'.
Portuguese ships bring chilies to the islands of the spice trade.
Gao Lian's Eight Discourses mentions 'foreign pepper', grown for its red fruit. Only in the eighteenth century does China cook with it, above all in Hunan and Sichuan.
Yi Su-gwang's encyclopedia calls it 'Japanese mustard', a poison brought from Japan. A century later it is in kimchi.

name: Tobacco
summary: Across the Americas tobacco is smoked, chewed and snuffed: in prayer, in healing and to seal agreements. Within a century of Columbus it is smoked from London to Beijing, and rulers from the Ottoman sultan to the Chinese emperor try and fail to ban it.

spread.note: Rodrigo de Jerez and Luis de Torres see people in Cuba smoking rolled leaves.
Tobacco is grown in Lisbon gardens as a medicinal plant.
Jean Nicot, the French ambassador in Lisbon, sends tobacco to Catherine de' Medici as a cure for headaches. Nicotine is named after him.
Thomas Harriot learns to smoke from the Algonquian people of Roanoke and praises it in his Briefe and True Report.
Portuguese sailors bring tobacco; within a few years the shogunate tries, and fails, to ban it.
Tobacco reaches the Ottoman capital. In 1633 Murad IV bans smoking on pain of death.
English merchants bring it to Muscovy. Tsar Mikhail bans it in 1634; Peter the Great later sells the monopoly to an English lord.
Tobacco reaches Fujian from Spanish Manila. The Chongzhen emperor bans it in 1639; his soldiers in the north smoke it against the cold.
Tobacco comes from Japan through the trading post at Busan, and within years everyone smokes.
Tobacco reaches the Mongols through Chinese and Russian traders.
Hopewell pipes carved in stone, for tobacco smoked in ceremony.
Tobacco, burned to carry words to the Creator.
Asad Beg presents tobacco and a jewelled pipe to Akbar, who tries it despite his physicians.
Tobacco is grown and smoked in Java.

name: Cacao
summary: Cacao is first used in the upper Amazon, but it is in Mesoamerica that it becomes the frothy drink of kings and gods, and its beans serve as small change in Aztec markets. Europe sweetens it with sugar; Africa now grows most of it.

spread.note: Potters on the Pacific coast of Mesoamerica leave cacao residue in their drinking vessels.
Cacao residue in spouted jars at Colha in Belize, the oldest in the Maya world. The Maya name, kakaw, passes into Nahuatl and then into every European language.
Cortés's men see Moctezuma served chocolate in golden cups.
A delegation of Maya nobles brings chocolate to the Spanish court; within a century it is the fashion there.
By tradition Anne of Austria brings the Spanish taste for chocolate to Paris when she marries Louis XIII.
London's first chocolate house opens, selling 'an excellent West India drink'.
Tetteh Quarshie brings cacao pods home from Fernando Po. West Africa becomes the world's largest grower.

name: The turkey
summary: Domesticated in Mexico for its meat and feathers. In Europe and Asia nobody knew where it came from: the English named it after Turkey, the French called it the bird of the Indies, and the Turks the bird of India.

spread.note: Turkey bones from central Mexico at El Mirador. The Maya already hunted their own wild ocellated turkey.
King Ferdinand orders every ship from the Indies to bring ten turkeys.
Turkeys reach England, named for the Turkish merchants who were thought to have brought them.
The French call it the dinde, the bird d'Inde, of the Indies.
The Ottomans call it hindi, the Indian bird.
Ustad Mansur paints a turkey brought to Jahangir from Goa.

name: Tea
summary: Tea leaves found in the tomb of the Han emperor Jing, who died in 141 BCE, are the oldest known. By the Tang it is China's national drink. It reached the rest of the world by three roads: to Japan with monks, across the steppe by caravan, and to Europe by sea.

spread.note: Uyghur envoys trade horses for tea at the Tang court and carry it home.
The monk Saichō brings tea seeds home from Tang China.
The envoy Kim Daeryeom brings tea seeds back from the Tang, and the king has them planted on Mount Jiri.
A Gulf merchant's account of China describes a herb the Chinese drink in hot water, called sakh.
The monk Eisai brings home Song-style powdered tea, the root of the tea ceremony.
Giovanni Battista Ramusio prints a Persian merchant's account of chai catai, the tea of Cathay.
The Dutch East India Company lands the first shipment of tea in Europe.
The tsar's envoy Vasily Starkov brings back tea as a gift from the Mongol Altan Khan. Tea comes to Russia by caravan for the next two centuries.
The first advertisement for tea in London; Catherine of Braganza makes it the drink of the court.
Chinese junks bring tea to Batavia, where the Dutch buy it for Europe.
The Singpho chief Bessa Gam shows Robert Bruce the wild tea of Assam. Tea gardens soon cover the hills of India.

name: Coffee
summary: Coffee grows wild in the forests of southwest Ethiopia. Sufis in Yemen are the first known to roast and brew it, to stay awake through their night prayers; from Mocha it spread through the Islamic world and then to Europe's coffeehouses.

spread.note: The Sufis of Yemen drink coffee for their night devotions. The port of Mocha gives its name to the trade.
Yemeni students drink coffee at al-Azhar. In 1511 the governor of Mecca tries to ban it.
The first coffeehouses open in Istanbul.
Venetian merchants bring coffee from the Ottoman ports.
Pasqua Rosée, a servant from Smyrna, opens London's first coffeehouse.
Süleyman Ağa, the sultan's envoy, serves coffee to Paris society.
By legend the Sufi Baba Budan smuggles seven beans from Mocha and plants them in the hills of Karnataka.
The Dutch plant coffee on Java, and 'java' becomes a word for coffee.
Francisco de Melo Palheta brings seedlings from French Guiana. Brazil becomes the world's largest grower.
King Gojong drinks coffee while sheltering in the Russian legation.

name: Sugar cane
summary: First grown in New Guinea, sugar cane spread to India, where people learned to boil its juice into crystals; the Sanskrit khanda gave the world 'candy'. The Atlantic plantations that grew it were worked by enslaved Africans.

spread.note: Cane is grown on the Ganges plain. By about 350 CE Indians crystallise its juice into sugar.
Alexander's admiral Nearchus reports a reed in India that gives honey without bees.
Cane is grown and refined in Khuzistan.
The Tang emperor Taizong sends to Magadha to learn how Indians boil cane into sugar.
The Arab conquests carry cane to Egypt, and on to Sicily and al-Andalus.
The monk Ganjin is said to have brought cane sugar to Japan among his medicines.
Cane grows on the coast of al-Andalus.
Sugar comes to Korea from China, a rare medicine and luxury.
Sugar and other luxuries cross the Sahara with the caravans.
Sugar cane is grown in the towns of the Swahili coast.
Sugar is made and taxed across Mongol-ruled China.
Portuguese planters on Madeira set up the first Atlantic sugar plantations.
Columbus brings cane to Hispaniola on his second voyage.
The first sugar mills are built near Veracruz.
Brazil becomes the world's largest producer of sugar, on the labour of enslaved Africans.

name: The silkworm
summary: Chinese farmers domesticate the silk moth, which can no longer fly, and learn to unwind its cocoon as a single thread. For centuries Rome bought silk without knowing what made it; Virgil thought it was combed from leaves.

spread.note: Indian texts name cīnapaṭṭa, cloth of silk from China.
The Han send the Xiongnu silk each year under the heqin treaties.
The Mahan raise silkworms and weave silk, say the Chinese histories.
The Wei chronicle records that the people of Wa raise silkworms.
By legend a Chinese princess, married to the king of Khotan, smuggles silkworm eggs out in her headdress.
Persia weaves silk and controls its trade between China and Rome.
Two monks smuggle silkworm eggs to Justinian in hollow canes, ending Persia's hold on the silk trade.
The Türk khagan sends Maniakh to Constantinople to sell silk directly to the Romans.
Chinese silk is traded at the ports of Srivijaya.
The Rus treaty with Constantinople limits how much silk Rus merchants may buy.
Al-Andalus raises silkworms on mulberry, and Almería's silks are famous across the Mediterranean.
Francis I grants Lyon the privileges that make it Europe's silk city.

name: The horse
summary: Herders of the western steppe breed the horse that every domestic horse descends from. Within a few centuries it spreads across Eurasia, pulling chariots and later carrying riders. In the Americas, where horses had died out ten thousand years before, Europeans brought them back.

spread.note: The Hyksos bring the horse and chariot into Egypt.
Chariots appear on the gravestones of Mycenae.
The Rigveda praises horses and chariots.
Horses and chariots are buried in Shang royal tombs.
Horse skulls ring the deer stones and stone mounds of the Mongolian steppe: its herders now ride.
Horse fittings appear in the graves of the north.
Horses come to Japan from Korea; the great tombs of the Kofun age are ringed with clay horses.
Horses and riders are carved on the reliefs of Borobudur.
Columbus's second voyage brings the first horses back to the Americas.
The Mexica see horses for the first time; Cortés's sixteen horses count for more in battle than their numbers.
Cortés leaves a lame horse with the Itza king. It dies, and the Itza make a stone statue of it, which friars find and smash in 1618.
Pizarro's riders charge at Cajamarca, and the Inca meet the horse.
Horses spread north from New Mexico after the Pueblo Revolt; the Comanche, Lakota and Cheyenne become horse peoples.
De Soto's army brings some two hundred horses through the Southeast.

name: The giraffe
summary: The tallest animal on earth. For peoples far from Africa it was a creature of report, gift and legend: a camel spotted like a leopard to the Romans, an auspicious qilin to the Ming court.

spread.note: Julius Caesar shows a giraffe at his games, the first seen in Europe. The Romans call it camelopardalis.
A giraffe from Malindi reaches the sultan of Bengal, who sends it on to the Yongle emperor.
A giraffe from Malindi, by way of Bengal, is presented to the Yongle emperor and greeted as a qilin.
The Mamluk sultan sends a giraffe to Lorenzo de' Medici; it becomes the pride of Florence.
Zarafa, a gift from Muhammad Ali of Egypt to Charles X, walks from Marseille to Paris; crowds come to see her.
Another of Muhammad Ali's giraffes reaches George IV at Windsor.

name: The rhinoceros
summary: Rhinoceroses lived across Africa and South and Southeast Asia, and in south China into historic times. Europe's picture of one for two centuries came from a woodcut by an artist who never saw it.

spread.note: Ctesias, a Greek doctor at the Persian court, describes a one-horned 'Indian wild ass', one root of the unicorn.
Pompey shows a rhinoceros at his games.
Rhinoceros horn comes to Korea from China as medicine and ornament.
Rhinoceros horn is among the medicines dedicated to Tōdai-ji and kept in the Shōsōin.
Al-Biruni describes the Indian rhinoceros and its single horn.
Ganda, a gift from the sultan of Gujarat, lands in Lisbon, the first rhinoceros in Europe since Roman times.
From a letter and a sketch, Dürer cuts his woodcut of a rhinoceros in armour plate.
The first rhinoceros in England is shown in London.

name: The kangaroo
summary: Hunted and honoured by Australia's first peoples for tens of thousands of years. To Europeans it looked like nothing made anywhere else: an animal the size of a deer that went about on two legs and carried its young in a pouch.

spread.note: Shipwrecked on the Abrolhos, the Batavia's commander Francisco Pelsaert describes a tammar wallaby, the first written account of a kangaroo.
Macassan trepangers working the coast of northern Australia meet its people and animals.
Cook's men shoot one and learn its name, gangurru, from the Guugu Yimithirr people.
Baudin's expedition brings live kangaroos home for Joséphine's gardens at Malmaison.

name: The dodo

extinct.note: Last seen in 1662, by castaways from the Dutch ship Arnhem.

summary: A flightless pigeon larger than a turkey, which lived only on Mauritius and had never met a predator. Within seventy years of the first sailors it was gone: the first extinction people later recognised they had caused.

spread.note: Wybrand van Warwijck's Dutch fleet lands on Mauritius; the sailors call the bird walghvogel, 'loathsome bird', for its tough meat.
A dodo at the Mughal court is painted, probably by Ustad Mansur.
Hamon L'Estrange sees a live dodo shown in a London house.
A Dutch ship brings a live dodo to Dejima at Nagasaki.

name: The giant panda
summary: The giant panda lives only in the bamboo forests of the mountains west of Sichuan. Outside China it was unknown until 1869; seventy years later it was the most famous animal in the world.

spread.note: Hunters show the missionary-naturalist Armand David a panda's skin, and he sends specimens to Paris.
Su Lin, the first live panda outside China, reaches Chicago with Ruth Harkness.
Pandas arrive at London Zoo; one, Ming, becomes a wartime favourite.

name: The coelacanth
summary: A lobe-finned fish known from fossils four hundred million years old, and thought to have died out with the dinosaurs, until a living one was caught off South Africa in 1938. Comorian fishermen had been catching it all along.

spread.note: Louis Agassiz names the coelacanths from fossils, a group thought extinct for sixty-six million years.
Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer finds a strange blue fish in a trawler's catch; J. L. B. Smith recognises a living coelacanth.

name: The tulip
summary: Wild tulips grow in the mountains of Central Asia. Persian poets and Ottoman gardeners made it the flower of paradise, and in Holland in 1637 a single bulb could cost as much as a house.

spread.note: The gardens of the Ottoman sultans fill with tulips.
Babur counts the kinds of tulip on the hills around Kabul.
Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq, the Habsburg envoy, sees tulips in Turkish gardens and sends bulbs home.
Carolus Clusius plants tulips in Leiden's botanical garden.
Tulip mania peaks and crashes.

name: Rice
summary: Farmers of the lower Yangtze tame a wild marsh grass into rice, grown in flooded fields. It came to feed more people than any other crop.

spread.note: Mumun farmers grow rice in paddy fields in the southwest of the peninsula.
Wet-field rice comes to Kyushu from Korea, and with it the Yayoi age.
Rice is grown in Mesopotamia and Persia under the Achaemenids.
Alexander's officer Aristobulus describes rice growing in water in India.
Farmers of the inland Niger delta grow African rice, a cousin of Asian rice tamed on the Niger.
Asian rice is grown on the Swahili coast and in Madagascar.
Rice is grown in the irrigated huertas of al-Andalus; Spanish arroz comes from the Arabic al-ruzz.
With the fall of Zhongdu the Mongols hold the rice-eating lands of northern China.
Rice becomes the crop of the Carolina low country, grown on the knowledge and labour of enslaved West Africans.

name: Wheat
summary: Einkorn and emmer, the first wheats, are domesticated in the hills of the Fertile Crescent, and bread wheat follows. Wheat travels with the first farmers into Europe, North Africa and India, and east along the steppe to China.

spread.note: Wheat reaches the Hexi corridor from the west; in time it becomes the grain of north China's noodles and steamed buns.
Wheat and barley grow alongside millet and rice in Mumun villages.
Wheat and barley reach Japan by way of Korea.
Juan Garrido, an African conquistador, is said to have sown the first wheat in Mexico, from a few grains found in a sack of rice.
Inés Muñoz sows the first wheat in Peru.

name: The banana

origin.culture: Farmers of the New Guinea highlands

summary: Bananas were first cultivated in New Guinea, and carried by Austronesian voyagers from Island Southeast Asia west to Africa and east across the Pacific. From the Canaries, Spain took them to the Americas.

spread.note: Bananas are grown in India, where the Buddhist texts later use the plantain's stem, layer upon layer with no core, as an image of the self.
Lapita voyagers carry bananas into the Pacific.
Alexander's men see a tree whose fruit the Indian sages live on; Pliny calls it pala.
Chinese writers describe the banana, bajiao, of the far south.
Bananas reach East Africa, probably with the Austronesian sailors who settled Madagascar, and become a staple of the great lakes.
Portuguese and Spanish settlers bring bananas from West Africa to the Canaries.
The friar Tomás de Berlanga brings banana roots from Gran Canaria to Santo Domingo.
Bananas, carried across Africa from the Indian Ocean, become a staple of the forest edge.
Arab growers carry the banana, mawz, from India to Oman, Egypt and later Spain.

name: The sweet orange
summary: A cross of the pomelo and the mandarin, bred in southern China. Sour oranges and lemons came west with the Arabs; the sweet orange came by sea with the Portuguese, and across the Mediterranean it is still named after Portugal.

spread.note: Citrus fruits grow in the hills of north-eastern India, near their home.
Citrus trees are planted at the Japanese court.
Jeju sends citrus fruit to the Goryeo court as tribute.
Citrus fruits are grown in Java.
Portuguese ships bring sweet oranges from China. In Greek the fruit becomes portokali, in Turkish portakal, in Arabic burtuqal.
The Ottomans call the sweet orange portakal, the Portuguese fruit.
Spanish settlers plant oranges in Florida.
Louis XIV's great orangery at Versailles houses more than a thousand orange trees in tubs.

name: Cassava
summary: A root that is poisonous until it is grated, soaked and cooked, domesticated on the southern edge of the Amazon. Carried from Brazil to Africa by Portuguese ships, it became the staple of central Africa.

spread.note: Manioc grows in the fields of Cerén, buried by a volcano about 600 CE.
Pero Vaz de Caminha writes of the root the Tupi make their bread from.
Portuguese ships bring cassava from Brazil to the Kongo coast, where it becomes the staple of central Africa.
Cassava is grown on the Swahili coast.

name: The tomato
summary: A wild Andean berry, domesticated in Mexico. Europe grew it for two centuries as a curiosity, half suspected of being poisonous, before Naples made it a sauce.

spread.note: Pietro Andrea Mattioli describes the pomi d'oro, golden apples, in his herbal.
John Gerard grows 'apples of love' but thinks them rank and stinking.
Wang Xiangjin's book of plants lists the fanshi, the 'foreign persimmon', as an ornamental.
Kanō Tan'yū paints the tōgaki, the 'Chinese persimmon', grown for its looks.

name: Black pepper
summary: The berry of a vine of the Malabar coast, and for two thousand years the most valuable spice in the world's trade. Rome, Venice and Lisbon each grew rich on it in turn.

spread.note: Peppercorns are placed in the nostrils of the mummy of Ramesses II.
Roman ships load pepper at Muziris; Pliny complains that India drains the empire of fifty million sesterces a year.
Aksum's port of Adulis trades with India, pepper among the goods.
Tang cooks use hujiao, the 'foreign pepper', brought by sea from India.
Pepper is among the medicines dedicated to Tōdai-ji and kept in the Shōsōin.
Pepper from Malabar is traded along the Swahili coast.
Pepper comes to Rus by the river roads from the Black Sea and the Caspian.
Pepper reaches the Mongol court in great quantity by sea.
Envoys from Chūzan bring pepper and sappanwood to the Goryeo court.
Pepper is planted in Sumatra and western Java, and Banten becomes a great pepper port.
Vasco da Gama reaches the pepper coast by sea, and Lisbon breaks Venice's hold on the trade.

name: Cloves and nutmeg
summary: Cloves grew only on a few islands of the northern Moluccas, and nutmeg only in the tiny Banda Islands. Wars were fought across the world for them.

spread.note: Han courtiers chew cloves to sweeten their breath before they speak to the emperor.
Pliny describes caryophyllon, an Indian spice like a peppercorn.
Cloves come by sea to the ports of India, where Sanskrit calls them lavanga.
Cloves are among the medicines dedicated to Tōdai-ji and kept in the Shōsōin.
Gulf merchants trading to China list cloves among the goods of the eastern islands.
Cloves reach Goryeo with Chinese and Arab merchants.
Magellan's surviving ships load cloves at Tidore; the cargo of the Victoria pays for the whole voyage.
English traders hold the tiny nutmeg island of Run. In 1667 England gives it up to the Dutch and keeps Manhattan.
The Dutch seize Banda for its nutmeg, killing or enslaving most of its people.
Pierre Poivre smuggles clove and nutmeg seedlings to Mauritius, ending the Dutch monopoly.

name: Rubber
summary: Mesoamericans made balls of rubber three and a half thousand years ago. The Amazon's rubber tree made fortunes after 1850, until seeds taken to Asia ended Brazil's hold on the trade.

spread.note: Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo describes the bouncing balls of the island ballgame.
La Condamine sends samples of caoutchouc to the Paris Academy.
Joseph Priestley finds that it rubs out pencil marks, and calls it rubber.
Henry Wickham ships seventy thousand rubber seeds from the Amazon to Kew Gardens.
Seedlings from Kew reach Singapore; within forty years the plantations of Malaya and Sumatra grow most of the world's rubber.

name: Cinchona and quinine
summary: The bark of a tree of the eastern Andes, the first effective remedy for malaria. Quinine, drawn from it in 1820, let Europeans live, trade and conquer in the tropics.

spread.note: Jesuits bring the bark to Rome, and the apothecary of their college gives it to the city's fever patients: 'Jesuits' powder'.
The English quack Robert Talbor cures the Dauphin with the bark, and Louis XIV buys his secret.
French Jesuits cure the Kangxi emperor's fever with the bark.
The Dutch smuggle cinchona seeds out of South America and plant them on Java, which comes to supply most of the world's quinine.
Clements Markham's seedlings from Peru are planted at Ootacamund.

name: The cat
summary: Wildcats move into the grain stores of the first farmers and stay. Egypt made the cat sacred, and ships carried cats round the world to keep down the rats.

spread.note: Cats appear on Greek vases and reliefs, still a rare and foreign pet.
Domestic cats from the west reach China, replacing the leopard cats Chinese farmers had once kept.
Cats come to Korea from China.
Emperor Uda writes in his diary of his black cat, brought from China: the first Japanese account of a pet cat.
Cats are kept in Java.
Cats are kept in the towns of Rus.
Ships' cats come ashore in the Americas.

name: The chicken

origin.culture: Rice farmers of mainland Southeast Asia

summary: The red junglefowl, drawn to the rice fields of Southeast Asia, becomes the chicken. It spread west across Asia to the Mediterranean and east in Polynesian canoes across the Pacific, perhaps as far as South America.

spread.note: Chickens are kept in India.
Chickens are kept in Shang and Zhou China.
The annals of Thutmose III record a bird 'that gives birth every day' sent as tribute.
The Greeks call it the Persian bird.
Chickens are kept in the Horn of Africa.
Chickens reach Japan, kept for their crowing at dawn as much as for food.
The Chinese histories describe the long-tailed chickens of the Mahan in the southwest.
Chickens are kept in the villages of the Niger bend.
Chickens are kept in the towns of the Swahili coast.
Chickens travel across the Pacific in the voyaging canoes.
Chickens are kept in the villages of west-central Africa.
Chicken bones on the coast of Chile may predate Columbus, brought by Polynesian voyagers; the dating is disputed.
Spanish chickens join the Maya's own turkeys in village yards.

name: The elephant
summary: Tamed in India for work and war, and hunted in Africa for ivory. Far from home, a single elephant could be a king's most famous gift.

spread.note: Darius brings fifteen war elephants to Gaugamela, the first the Macedonians have faced.
Pyrrhus's elephants rout the Roman cavalry; the Romans call them 'Lucanian oxen'.
Abul-Abbas, an elephant sent by the caliph Harun al-Rashid, reaches Charlemagne.
Louis IX gives Henry III an elephant, kept at the Tower; Matthew Paris draws it from life.
Kublai Khan rides into battle against the rebel Nayan in a tower carried by four elephants.
A ship from Palembang brings an elephant to Japan as a gift for the shogun.
The shogun sends King Taejong an elephant. After it tramples a man to death it is banished to an island.
Hanno, an Indian elephant from King Manuel of Portugal, is presented to Pope Leo X.

name: The polar bear
summary: The great white bear of the Arctic ice, hunted and revered by the Inuit. Medieval kings traded live ones as the rarest of gifts.

spread.note: King Haakon of Norway sends Henry III a white bear, kept at the Tower and let out on a long chain to fish in the Thames.
Live polar bears from the Arctic coast are kept at the court of Empress Anna.

name: The moa

extinct.note: Hunted out within about two centuries of the first settlers.

summary: Giant flightless birds, the tallest up to three metres, that lived only in New Zealand. The first people to arrive hunted them to extinction in a few generations.

spread.note: The first settlers hunt moa; their camp at Wairau Bar is littered with moa bones and eggshell.
From a single thigh bone sent from New Zealand, Richard Owen deduces a giant bird, long extinct.

name: The okapi

origin.culture: The Mbuti and Efe of the Ituri

summary: A shy forest relative of the giraffe, striped like a zebra on its legs. Known to the forest peoples of the Ituri, it was one of the last large mammals the outside world learned of.

spread.note: Henry Morton Stanley hears of a forest animal like a donkey that the Mbuti catch in pits.
Harry Johnston sends a skin and two skulls to London, and the okapi is named.

name: The peanut

origin.culture: Farmers of the western Andean foothills

summary: A legume that flowers above ground and ripens its pods below it. Bred from wild peanuts of the eastern Andean foothills, it is grown in northern Peru by about 6000 BCE. After 1500 Portuguese ships carry it to Africa and Asia, where it becomes a staple and a source of oil.

spread.note: The lord of Sipán, a Moche ruler, is buried with a necklace of gold and silver peanuts.
Peanuts, tlalcacahuatl, 'earth cacao', are sold in the markets of Tenochtitlan.
Oviedo describes maní, grown by the Taíno of Hispaniola.
Peanuts appear in the local gazetteers of the lower Yangzi, brought by sea.
Portuguese ships bring peanuts from Brazil to West Africa, where they become a field crop.
The Portuguese bring peanuts to India.
Peanuts, nguba, are grown in Kongo and Angola.
Peanuts reach North America from Africa with enslaved Africans; nguba becomes 'goober'.

name: The soybean
summary: Farmers in northern China, Korea and Japan each select larger beans from a wild vine, and the soybean becomes one of East Asia's staple foods, eaten as soy sauce, tofu, miso and tempeh. It reaches Europe and the Americas only in the eighteenth century.

spread.note: Jōmon villagers in the mountains of central Japan grow soybeans larger than wild ones.
Farmers of the Mumun period in Korea grow soybeans and azuki beans.
Engelbert Kaempfer, back from Japan, describes the soybean and how miso and soy sauce are made.
Samuel Bowen, a sailor who had been to China, plants soybeans near Savannah to make soy sauce and noodles.
The Serat Centhini mentions tempe, a cake of fermented soybeans.

name: The coconut
summary: A palm whose seed floats and keeps its water for months at sea. People took it up twice, in Island Southeast Asia and around southern India; Austronesian voyagers carried it across the Pacific and the Indian Ocean, and it gave food, drink, oil, rope and timber to every tropical coast.

spread.note: Coconuts of the Indian Ocean kind are grown on the Malabar coast.
Chinese writers describe the coconut palm, yezi, of Hainan and the far south.
Coconuts of the Pacific kind reach the Swahili coast and Madagascar with Austronesian voyagers.
The Account of China and India describes the coconut palms of the islands on the way to China.
Marco Polo describes the 'Indian nuts', as big as a man's head, full of sweet liquor.
Ibn Battuta describes the Maldivian coconut palm: its fruit, its milk and the coir that sews the islanders' ships together.
Oviedo finds coconut palms already growing on the Pacific coast of Panama, perhaps carried there by the sea.

name: Sorghum

origin.culture: Herders and farmers of eastern Sudan

summary: A grass of the African savanna that thrives where it is too hot and dry for wheat or rice. People in eastern Sudan began to cultivate it about 3500 BCE; it crossed to India by 2000 BCE and became a staple from the Sahel to northern China.

spread.note: Sorghum crosses the Arabian Sea to western India, where it becomes jowar.
At Jenne-jeno, farmers grow sorghum alongside African rice and pearl millet.
Pliny writes of a millet brought from India within the last ten years, dark and large-grained: probably sorghum.
Sorghum is a staple of the highlands around Aksum.
Sorghum, dhurra, is grown in the highlands of Yemen.
Sorghum, gaoliang, spreads in northern China.
Sorghum, 'guinea corn', reaches the Americas with the Atlantic slave trade.

name: Breadfruit

origin.place: New Guinea and the Bismarck Archipelago

summary: A tree whose large starchy fruit is roasted, baked or fermented. Islanders of western Melanesia bred it, and Pacific voyagers carried seedless kinds, which grow only from cuttings, from island to island. Europeans saw it as cheap food; Britain sent the Bounty to fetch it.

spread.note: Voyagers carry breadfruit east across the Pacific to Tahiti and beyond.
William Dampier describes breadfruit on Guam: 'as big as a penny loaf'.
After the mutiny on the Bounty ended his first attempt, William Bligh brings breadfruit from Tahiti to St Vincent and Jamaica as cheap food for enslaved people.

name: The grapevine
summary: Farmers of the South Caucasus were making wine by 6000 BCE. The cultivated vine spread through the Near East and around the Mediterranean, where wine became part of feasts and worship; Han envoys took it to China, and Spanish and Dutch settlers to the Americas and southern Africa.

spread.note: Jars at Hajji Firuz Tepe in the Zagros hold the residue of wine flavoured with resin.
A king of Egypt is buried at Abydos with some seven hundred jars of wine from the Levant.
Linear B tablets at Knossos and Pylos record wine, wo-no.
Greek settlers at Massalia plant vines, and Gaul takes to wine.
Grapes and wine reach north-western India with Persian and Greek rule.
Zhang Qian brings word of grape wine in Dayuan; Han envoys bring back vines and plant them beside the palaces.
Grapes and grapevine patterns reach Japan from Tang China.
Grapevine patterns come to Silla from Tang China.
The Uyghurs of Turfan grow grapes and make wine.
Cortés orders Spanish settlers who hold Native labourers in encomienda to plant vines.
Garcilaso remembers the first grapes ripening in Cuzco.
Jan van Riebeeck records the first wine pressed from Cape grapes.

name: The olive
summary: A slow-growing tree of the dry Mediterranean hills, cultivated in the Levant by about 4500 BCE for its oil, which lit lamps, anointed bodies and cooked food. It spread with Phoenician and Greek settlers around the Mediterranean, and with the Spanish to the Americas.

spread.note: Minoan palaces store olive oil in great jars.
Tutankhamun is buried with wreaths of olive leaves; Egypt imports most of its oil.
Phoenician settlers plant olives in southern Iberia.
Pliny writes that there were no olives in Italy in the time of Tarquinius Priscus, about 580 BCE; Greek settlers bring them.
Duan Chengshi describes the qitun tree of Persia and Fulin, whose fruit is pressed for oil.
Antonio de Ribera brings olive saplings from Seville to Lima; Garcilaso tells how only three of a hundred survived the voyage.

name: The peach
summary: Farmers of the lower Yangzi chose larger and sweeter peaches over thousands of years, and the peach became China's fruit of long life. It travelled west along the routes to Persia, which the Romans thought was its home, and on with the Spanish to the Americas.

spread.note: More than two thousand peach stones are buried at Makimuku, perhaps offerings at an early royal court.
Peaches reach Persia along the routes from China; the Greeks will call them 'Persian apples'.
Peaches are grown in Korea.
Pliny writes of the persica, a fruit lately come to Italy, which travels badly.
Peaches come to Kashmir and the north-west along the routes from China.
The Mongols take the orchards of northern China with Zhongdu.
Peaches spread from Spanish Florida faster than the settlers, and Native towns of the Southeast grow them in orchards.

name: Vanilla

origin.culture: The Totonac of the Gulf coast

summary: The cured pod of a climbing orchid of the Gulf coast forests, grown by the Totonac. The Mexica flavoured chocolate with it, and Europe took it with chocolate. Outside Mexico the flowers would not set fruit until 1841, when an enslaved boy on Réunion found how to pollinate them by hand.

spread.note: The Mexica conquer the Totonac coast and take vanilla, tlilxochitl, 'black flower', as tribute to flavour chocolate.
Vanilla comes to Spain with cacao, to flavour chocolate as the Mexica did.
Hugh Morgan, apothecary to Elizabeth I, suggests vanilla as a flavouring on its own.
Edmond Albius, a twelve-year-old enslaved boy on Réunion, finds how to pollinate vanilla flowers by hand; it can now bear fruit far from the Mexican bees that do the work.
Planters carry vanilla from Réunion to Madagascar, which becomes its largest grower.

name: The dromedary
summary: The one-humped camel, tamed in south-east Arabia around 1100 BCE, can go days without water and carry heavy loads across sand. It carried the incense trade of Arabia, then the caravans of the Sahara, and in the nineteenth century it was taken to Australia to open the interior.

spread.note: The Rigveda names the camel, uṣṭra.
Gindibu the Arab brings a thousand camels to the battle of Qarqar, says an Assyrian inscription.
Cyrus sets camels against Croesus's cavalry at Sardis; the horses bolt at their smell, says Herodotus.
Camels come into common use in Egypt in Persian and Ptolemaic times.
Camels spread across Roman North Africa; in the 360s Leptis Magna is asked for four thousand.
Camel caravans cross the Sahara to Ghana, carrying salt south and gold north.
Camels and cameleers from Afghanistan and British India come to Australia; the Burke and Wills expedition sets out with two dozen.

name: The llama
summary: Herders of the high Andean grasslands tamed the wild guanaco into the llama, and the vicuña into the alpaca. Llamas carried the loads of the Andes, from the Inca roads to the silver of Potosí; their wool, meat and dung kept highland life going where few crops would grow.

spread.note: Francisco Pizarro brings llamas from Tumbes to show Charles V in Toledo.
Conrad Gessner prints a picture of the 'allocamelus', from a sketch of a llama.
Trains of llamas carry the silver ore of Potosí and the goods of its markets.

name: The dog
summary: The first animal people tamed, from wolves, in Ice Age Eurasia; where exactly is still argued, but a dog was buried with two people at Bonn-Oberkassel some fourteen thousand years ago. Dogs went with the first people into the Americas, and later with voyagers to Australia and across the Pacific.

spread.note: Dogs are buried with care at Koster in the Illinois valley, among the oldest dog graves in the Americas; dogs had come with the first people.
The dingo reaches Australia by sea, perhaps with voyagers from Island Southeast Asia; the oldest dingo bones are at Madura Cave.
Thule people cross the Arctic to Greenland with dog sleds.
Voyagers bring the kurī, a Polynesian dog, to Aotearoa.

name: The pig
summary: Wild boar were tamed at least twice, in eastern Anatolia and in China, and pigs became the meat of farming villages across Eurasia. Lapita voyagers carried them into the Pacific; Columbus and de Soto brought them to the Americas, where escaped herds ran wild.

spread.note: Farmers at Jiahu keep pigs tamed separately from the boars of the Near East.
Pigs reach Korea from China.
Lapita voyagers carry pigs, dogs and chickens into the Pacific.
Columbus brings eight pigs from the Canary Islands to Hispaniola.
Hernando de Soto lands in Florida with thirteen sows; by his death the herd numbers some seven hundred.

name: The European rabbit
summary: The European rabbit lived wild only in Iberia and southern France; Phoenician sailors may have named Spain for it, taking it for the hyrax of home. Romans kept it in walled warrens, monks and lords bred it, and in 1859 two dozen rabbits let loose in Australia became hundreds of millions.

spread.note: Pliny tells of rabbits so many on the Balearic Islands that the islanders asked Augustus for soldiers to fight them.
The Normans bring rabbits to Britain and keep them in warrens; the first records are from the Isles of Scilly.
Rabbits are bred in hutches in France, and the tame rabbit takes shape.
Thomas Austin releases twenty-four rabbits for hunting; within fifty years there are hundreds of millions across Australia.

name: Steller's sea cow

extinct.note: The last sea cows are killed on Bering Island, twenty-seven years after Steller described them.

summary: A giant relative of the manatee, up to eight metres long, which grazed on kelp in the cold shallows of the Commander Islands. Georg Steller described it after Bering's shipwreck in 1741; hunters of sea otters killed the last of them twenty-seven years later.

spread.note: Shipwrecked with Bering's crew, Georg Steller describes a sea cow up to eight metres long; the crew eat it to survive.
Steller's description, De bestiis marinis, is published in St Petersburg: nearly all that will ever be known of the living animal.

name: The great auk

extinct.note: The last known pair is killed on Eldey, off Iceland, for a collector.

summary: A flightless seabird of the North Atlantic, nearly a metre tall, that came ashore only to breed. Maritime Archaic people were buried with its beaks; sailors filled their boats with it on Funk Island. Collectors paid for the last skins, and the last known pair was killed in 1844.

spread.note: Norse settlers in Iceland call it geirfugl.
Thule hunters reaching Greenland take great auks along its coasts.
Jacques Cartier's men fill two boats with great auks on the Isle of Birds in less than half an hour.
Ole Worm keeps a tame great auk from the Faroes and publishes its picture.

name: The passenger pigeon

origin.place: The forests of eastern North America

extinct.note: Martha, the last passenger pigeon, dies at the Cincinnati Zoo.

summary: Perhaps the most numerous bird on Earth, flying in flocks that darkened the sky for days over the forests of eastern North America. Netted and shot by the million and sent to city markets by rail, it was gone from the wild by 1900; the last one died in a zoo in 1914.

spread.note: Jacques Cartier sees wood pigeons beyond number on Prince Edward Island.
Audubon watches a flock pass overhead for three days, darkening the sun.
Hunters ship birds by the trainload from a great nesting near Petoskey, one of the last.

name: The thylacine

extinct.note: Benjamin, the last known thylacine, dies at Hobart's Beaumaris Zoo.

summary: A striped, dog-like marsupial hunter, the "Tasmanian tiger". It vanished from mainland Australia about 3,200 years ago, after the dingo came, and lived on in Tasmania until settlers and a government bounty killed thousands; the last known one died in Hobart in 1936.

spread.note: Thylacines are painted on the rocks of Arnhem Land; on the mainland they die out about 3,200 years ago.
Tasman's men see tracks with 'claws like a tiger' on Tasmania.
George Harris describes the thylacine for the Linnean Society of London.
A Tasmanian government bounty pays for 2,184 dead thylacines.
